title: Intellectual Property Laws Amendment Bill 2013
portfolio: Industry, Innovation, Climate Change, Science, Research and Tertiary Education

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would change intellectual property laws covering government use of inventions, medicine exports, plant breeders' rights and patent processes shared with New Zealand.
Australian manufacturers could seek Federal Court licences to produce patented medicines for export to eligible developing countries, with compensation for patent holders.
Patent applications could be examined jointly across Australia and New Zealand, while each country would continue granting separate patents under its own laws.
changes: Plant breeders could pursue infringement proceedings in the Federal Circuit Court.
Patent attorneys would be registered through a single trans-Tasman system with shared qualifications and disciplinary arrangements.
Specific document retention provisions would be repealed, leaving disposal governed by archives legislation.
Government use provisions in patent legislation would be clarified.
summary.affected: Patent applicants and holders, pharmaceutical manufacturers, plant breeders, patent attorneys and Australian and New Zealand patent authorities are affected.

speeches.speaker: Yvette D'Ath
speeches.brief: Moved the Intellectual Property Laws Amendment Bill 2013, clarifying Crown use provisions for patents in areas like health care, implementing the TRIPS protocol to let Australian manufacturers export generic medicines to developing countries citing a UN estimate that 260 million people were infected with malaria, HIV or tuberculosis in 2010 resulting in 3.6 million deaths, and establishing a first-of-its-kind single trans-Tasman patent examination and attorney regulation system with New Zealand.

speeches.speaker: Sophie Mirabella
speeches.brief: Argued that the Intellectual Property Laws Amendment Bill 2013 was rushed, poorly drafted and inadequately scrutinised despite its acceptable objectives. Raised concerns about Crown use, compulsory licences, the Australia-US FTA, TRIPS obligations, consultation and committee processes, and urged the government to withdraw and redraft the bill.

speeches.speaker: Melissa Parke
speeches.brief: Supported the Intellectual Property Laws Amendment Bill 2013 as an improvement to the patent system, particularly through clearer Crown use provisions, compulsory licensing for exporting medicines, plant breeders' rights reforms and a trans-Tasman patent attorney regime. Criticised patents over human genes and reported the United States Supreme Court decision on BRCA gene patents.

speeches.speaker: Dennis Jensen
speeches.brief: Opposed the Intellectual Property Laws Amendment Bill 2013 and called for more time and scrutiny, citing its complexity, limited committee consideration and inadequate consultation. Raised concerns about TRIPS provisions, possible unintended consequences, international obligations and rushed legislative processes.
